region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat', eBook #8299

summary.en: Down to seventy pesos, Juan deposits twenty in each of a town's three stores, contracting that a bow of his hat shall be payment. Publicly feasting at each, he sells the 'magic' hat to the highest bidder for five thousand pesos and sails away — while the buyer, bowing in a store he has not paid, is arrested, and faints with sickness on learning the simple trick.
summary.zh: 胡安僅剩七十比索，便向鎮上三家店鋪各存二十比索，約定『脫帽一躬即為付款』。他在各家當眾宴請、行禮離店，把『有魔法的帽子』以五千比索售予出價最高者，揚帆而去——而買主在他未存錢的店鋪行禮，遭店家喝令逮捕；聽聞這簡單的把戲後，當場昏厥。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Scheerer narrator (Manila); archival record. The 'hat pays' episode, imported from Europe where it is part of the Master-Cheat cycle (Bolte-Polívka on Grimm No. 61).

passages.text: There once lived a man by the name of Juan, who did nothing but fool people all the time. Once, when he had only seventy pesos left in his pockets, he determined to resort to the following scheme: he bought a balangut hat (a very cheap straw), and painted it five different colors. In the town where Juan was to operate there were only three stores; he went to each one of them and deposited twenty pesos, saying to the owner of each, 'I will deposit twenty pesos in your store, and to-morrow afternoon I will bring some friends here with me. We will perhaps take some refreshments or buy some goods, but in any case I will see to it that the total amount of the things we take is not over the twenty pesos. Then, when we leave, do not ask me to pay you for the things. I will simply make you a bow with my hat, and your attendants should thank me with much courtesy. That mere bow with my hat is to be the payment. You may keep the twenty pesos, but you must also keep this little plan a secret.' The owners of the three stores promised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day Juan was walking in the street with his painted hat on, when one of his friends met him: 'Halloo, Juan! Where did you get that funny hat?' Juan looked serious, and said, 'Don't be foolish! Don't you know that this hat is the only means I have of earning a living? Why, of course. I can go in any store, take anything I please, and pay for it with a mere bow of my hat.' By this time two other friends of Juan had come along, and they too were surprised to see what Juan had on his head; to convince them of the marvellous character of the hat, Juan took his friends to one of the stores, where they sat down and Juan ordered some refreshments; they ate much, and of the best that the store could furnish — then Juan stood up, made a bow to the proprietor with his hat, and they all left, the same thing taking place in another store.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The friends of Juan were very much astonished, and each wished to possess the hat: one offered him a thousand pesos for it; another, two thousand; and the third, one-half of all his property, which amounted to about five thousand pesos. Juan, of course, was willing to sell it to the highest bidder; but when the sale was about to be concluded, the buyer began to doubt the power of the hat, so he asked Juan to take him to another store to prove once more the qualities of the hat — and Juan took his friend to the third store, and the friend was now sure that the hat could really work wonders. So he paid Juan the five thousand pesos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he had received the money, Juan left his friends, went on board ship, and sailed away to a foreign country. One day the friend who had bought the hat desired to make a showing with it; so he invited several friends, among them some ladies, took them to one of the stores, and ordered some refreshments to be served — and when they had finished, the man bowed with his hat and started to leave. 'Thank you, sir! But where is my payment for the refreshments you have just eaten?' The owner of the hat was astonished, and, thinking that perhaps he held the hat in the wrong way, or else his fingers were not on the right color, he turned the hat around and made another bow; the owner of the shop now became angry and began to swear at the man, who, excited, twirled the hat around and held it in as many different ways as he could think of — finally the shop-keeper ordered the man arrested. When the owner of the hat heard how Juan had played his trick by paying twenty pesos in advance, he fainted and became very sick; in the meantime Juan was performing other tricks in some different country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan and Clotilde: The Ladder of Nails and the Matched Necklaces
title.zh: 胡安與克洛蒂爾德：釘梯與相配的項鍊

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog Märchen; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dying magician locks Princess Clotilde and three winged horses in a tower 'inaccessible to any human being'; kings' sons fail, but the peasant Juan builds a ladder of nails and rope, receives one of her two matchless necklaces, and flees a winged horse to a strange land when his treacherous brother pulls out the nails. Years later, hired as a farmhand, he borrows the princess's necklace from his adopted father and hammers an exact match — 'By the aid of the Lord! My lover is here again' — and the festivities continue nine days and nine nights before Juan succeeds to the throne.
summary.zh: 垂死的魔法師把公主克洛蒂爾德與三匹有翼馬鎖進『凡人不可攀』的高塔；諸王子皆敗，農夫胡安卻以長釘與繩索搭成釘梯登頂，得公主一條無雙項鍊；惡兄拔釘斷路，他乘飛馬飄落異鄉。多年後，他藉義父之名借來公主的項鍊，徹夜鎚打出分毫不差的複製品——『上天保佑！我的愛人又來了』——婚宴連慶九日九夜，胡安終登王位。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog Märchen recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Fansler relates it to the eighteenth-century Spanish ballad by Alonso de Morales ('Las Princesas Encantadas'), itself founded on Oriental material transmitted by the Arabs.

passages.text: In ages vastly remote there lived in a distant land a king of such prowess and renown that his name was known throughout the four regions of the compass; his name was Ludovico, and his power was increased twofold by his attachment to an aged magician, to whom he was tied by strong bonds of friendship. Ludovico had an extremely lovely daughter by the name of Clotilde; ever since his arrival at the palace the magician had been passionately in love with her, but his extreme old age and his somewhat haughty bearing were obstacles in his path to success, and whenever he made love to her she turned aside and listened instead to the thrilling tales told by some wandering minstrel. The magician finally succumbed to the infirmities of old age, his life made more burdensome by his repeated disappointments; he left to the king three enchanted winged horses, to the princess two magic necklaces of exactly the same appearance, of inimitable workmanship and of priceless worth — and before he expired he locked Clotilde and the three magic horses in a high tower inaccessible to any human being, where she was to remain in this enchanted prison until some man succeeded in setting her free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Naturally, King Ludovico wanted to see his daughter before the hour of his death, which was fast approaching; he offered large sums of money, together with his crown and Clotilde's hand, to anybody who could set her free. Hundreds of princes tried, but in vain: the stone walls of the tower were of such a height that very few birds, even, could fly over them. But a deliverer now rose from obscurity: this man was an uneducated but persevering peasant named Juan, who possessed a graceful form, herculean frame, good heart, and unrivalled ingenuity. His two learned older brothers tried to scale the walls of the tower but fared no better than the others; at last Juan's turn came, and though his parents and his older brothers expostulated with him not to go — for what could a man unskilled in the fine arts do? — Juan, in the hope of setting the princess free, paid no attention to their advice, and took as many of the biggest nails as he could find, a very long rope, and a strong hammer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Juan set out with all his equipment; on the way he met his disappointed second brother returning after a vain attempt, who tried in every way he could to divert Juan from his purpose. Juan's parents, actuated partly by a sense of shame if he should fail and partly by a deep-seated hatred, had poisoned his food without his knowledge; when he felt hungry he suspected them of some evil intention, so before eating he gave his horse some of his provisions — the poor creature died on the road amidst terrible sufferings, and Juan was obliged to finish the journey on foot. When he arrived at the foot of the tower, he drove a nail into the wall, then tied one end of his rope to this spike; in this way he succeeded in making a complete ladder of nails and rope to the top of the tower, where Clotilde met him with her eyes flooded with tears, giving him one of the magic necklaces as a reward for his great services.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While they were whispering words of love in each other's ears, they heard a deafening noise at the bottom of the tower: 'Rush for safety to your ladder!' cried Clotilde. 'One of the fiendish friends of the magician is going to kill you.' But, alas! Some wanton hand had pulled out the nails — and this person was none other than Juan's second brother. 'I am a lost man,' said Juan. 'Mount one of the winged horses in the chamber adjoining mine,' said Clotilde; so Juan got on one of the animals without knowing where to go, and the horse flew from the tower with such velocity that Juan had to close his eyes, his breath almost taken away — in a few seconds he was landed in a country entirely strange to his eyes. After long years of struggle with poverty and starvation, Juan was at last able to make his way back to his native country, and went to live in a town just outside the walls of the capital, where a rich old man named Telesforo hired him to work on his farm; Juan's excellent service and irreproachable conduct won the good will of his master, who adopted him as his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At about this time King Ludovico gave out proclamations stating that anyone who could exactly match his daughter's necklace should be his son-in-law; thousands tried, but they tried in vain — even the most dexterous and experienced smiths were baffled in their attempts to produce an exact counterfeit. When word of the royal proclamations was brought to Juan, he decided to try: one day he pretended to be sick and asked Telesforo to go to the palace to get Clotilde's necklace; the old man went that very afternoon and borrowed the necklace, so that he might try to copy it. After supper Juan went to his room and locked himself in, took from his pocket the necklace which Clotilde had given him in the tower, and compared it carefully with the borrowed one; when he saw that they did not differ in any respect, he took a piece of iron and hammered it until midnight. Early the next morning Juan wrapped the two magic necklaces in a silk handkerchief and told the old man to take them to the king. 'By the aid of the Lord!' exclaimed Clotilde when her father the king unwrapped the necklaces. 'My lover is here again. This necklace is not a counterfeit, for it is written in the magician's book of black art that no human being shall be able to imitate either of the magic necklaces. Where is the owner of this necklace, old man?' — 'He is at home,' said Telesforo with a bow. 'Go and bring him to the palace.' Within a quarter of an hour Juan arrived; after paying due respect to the king, Juan embraced Clotilde affectionately, and they were married in the afternoon, the festivities continuing for nine days and nine nights. Juan was made crown-prince, and on the death of King Ludovico he succeeded to the throne; King Juan and Queen Clotilde lived to extreme old age in peace and perfect happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Poor Man and His Three Sons: The Scythe, the Rooster, and the Cat
title.zh: 貧父與三子：鐮刀、雄雞與貓

region.en: Pasig, Rizal, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省帕西格（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dying father leaves each son one humble thing — a scythe, a rooster, a cat — 'which, if you will only be able to find a place in which it has no equal, will make you happy men.' The scythe is bought by rice-pullers amazed at its convenience; the time-crowing rooster by a town that has none; the rat-killing cat by a king whose palace it clears. All three return rich, having followed their father's wise advice: select the right place in which to trade.
summary.zh: 垂死的父親給三子各留一件平凡之物——鐮刀、雄雞、貓——『若能找到無可替代之地，便可致富。』拔稻而作的鄉民驚異於鐮刀之便；無雞的城鎮重金購下報時的雄雞；鼠患的王宮以鉅資買走捕鼠的貓。三兄弟皆富而歸——父親的遺訓是：貴在所售之地。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Velasquez narrator (Pasig); archival record. Imported from the Occident (Grimm No. 70 family; oldest form in Nicholas de Troyes, 1535); Fansler suspects introduction through a French religious.

passages.text: Once there lived a poor man who had three sons. When the father was on his death-bed, he called his sons and said to them, 'My sons, I shall die very soon; and I shall not be able to leave you much wealth, for wealth I have not. But I will give each one of you something which, if you will only be able to find a place in which it has no equal, will make you happy men.' The father then gave to one a rooster, to another a cat, and to the third a scythe; then he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The owner of the scythe was the first to try his fortune and test his father's advice: he left his brothers and went on a journey until he came to a town where he saw the people harvesting rice by pulling the stalks out of the ground. He showed the people the convenience of the scythe; they were so delighted and astonished that they offered to give him a large sum of money in exchange for the tool — of course he was willing to sell it, and he went home a rich man. The owner of the rooster, seeing the good luck of his brother, next resolved to try his fortune with the bird; like his brother, he travelled until he came to a town where there was no rooster. The people were very much interested in the rooster's crowing, and asked the owner why the bird crowed; he said that the bird told the time of day by its crowing — 'The first crow in the night announces midnight; the second, three o'clock in the morning; and the third crow announces five o'clock.' The people were very anxious to get the rooster for their town and offered to buy it; the owner was willing, and he returned to his home as rich as his brother who had sold the scythe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The last brother now set out to try his luck with his cat; at last he came to a town where the rats were vexing the people very much. He showed them the use of his cat; with wonder the people watched the cat kill the rats, and were astounded to see how the rats fled from this strange animal. The news of the cat reached the king, who summoned its owner to the palace; the king asked the brother to try his cat on the rats in the palace, and so the cat was turned loose — in a short time all the rats had either been killed or driven away. The king wanted the cat, and offered to pay a large sum of money for it; so the owner of the cat, after the king had paid him, went home as rich as his other two brothers. Thus the three brothers became rich, because they followed their father's wise advice: select the right place in which to trade.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog verse tale sung by a beggar with a guitar; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother', eBook #8299

summary.en: The king's pet dog bears three human daughters — Feliza, Juana, Maria — each married to a prince of a different kingdom. After the king's death their dog-mother, cast out of the palace, travels to each in turn: Feliza kicks her down the ladder, Juana has her tied in a distant forest — only Maria, finding her crying and yelping, unties her with her own hands, wraps her veil around her, and brings her home: 'this dog that I am carrying is my mother.' Light floods the dining-room, the dog disappears, and in its place stands a beautiful woman in glorious attire: 'I am the dog your mother. God bless you, my good child!'
summary.zh: 國王的愛犬生下三個人形女兒——菲莉莎、胡安娜、瑪利亞——分嫁三國王子。國王死後，狗母被逐出宮，輾轉尋女：菲莉莎把她踢下扶梯；胡安娜命衛士將她縛於遠林；唯瑪利亞聞其哀鳴，親手解縛、以面紗裹之載回王宮——『我懷中的狗，是我的母親。』餐廳驟亮，狗影化為華服美人：『我是你那狗身的母親。上帝保佑你，我的好孩子！』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale sung in Tagalog verse by a beggar with a guitar, framed by Fansler as heard on the road to a bone-setter; archival record. Fansler offers no close parallels, though the roles are reversed in Frere's Indian 'A Funny Story' (No. 2).

passages.text: In a certain country there lived a king who had a pet dog; he loved the dog so much and treated it so kindly that, wherever he went, the dog followed him. In the course of time the dog gave birth to three puppies — the most striking thing about these new-born creatures was that they were real human beings in every particular; so the king ordered them to be baptized: the eldest sister was named Feliza, the second Juana, and the youngest Maria. When they grew up into beautiful young women, they married three princes, each of a different kingdom; after the marriage-festivities each went to live in the country of her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Feliza was very happy: she dressed elegantly, and had all that a woman of her rank could wish for. One day, when her husband was away from home, a lean, dirty, spectre-looking dog came to her — it was Feliza's mother, who, after the death of her master the king, had been cast out of the palace; the poor dog had had nothing to eat for many days, had been driven away from every house, and had been frightened by mischievous boys with sticks and stones. Although Feliza's kingdom was very far away, she had managed, in spite of difficulty, to reach it, hoping to gain her daughter's pity. 'My daughter, have compassion on me! I, your mother, am in a very wretched condition.' 'What care I? What business have you to come here? Don't you know that I will never sacrifice anything for your sake? Get out of here!' — and she kicked the poor dog until it fell tumbling to the ground, for Feliza did not want her husband to find out that her mother was a dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sadly the dog went away, and decided to go to her daughter Juana's kingdom; the country was far away, but what else could she do? As Juana was coming out of the church with her husband, she saw the dog hurrying after her; like Feliza, she was ashamed of her mother, and whispered to one of the guards to catch the dog and tie it securely in a distant forest, so that it might no longer annoy her. Not long after this, Maria, the youngest daughter, was riding through the forest with her husband; there they found the poor dog crying and yelping in a pitiful manner. Maria recognized her mother: she got out of the carriage, and with her own hands untied the dog, wrapped her veil around it, and ordered the carriage to turn back to the palace. 'Husband, this dog that I am carrying is my mother, so please your Majesty.' The husband only said, 'Thank God!' and not another word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Maria ordered the cook to prepare delicious food for the dog, and assigned the best chamber in the palace to the animal; while the dog was eating with Maria, the prince, and the courtiers, the dining-room was suddenly illuminated with a bright light — the dog disappeared, and in its place stood a beautiful woman in glorious attire. The woman kissed Maria, and said, 'I am the dog your mother. God bless you, my good child!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.

region.en: Mexico, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town; pre-Spanish datu setting)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省墨西哥鎮（敘述者故鄉，西班牙時代前的達圖背景）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale (old Pampangan tradition); collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu', eBook #8299

summary.en: Datu Nebucheba covets his warrior Tomarind's beautiful wife and sends him twice to die: for an enchanted marble ball guarded by village-burning monsters, and to carry a letter to the datu's parents 'living under ground, in the realm of the spirits' — down a well to be buried under piled stones. The witch of Tipuca arms him with a magic cane and digs him a secret passage between the two wells; the 'answer' letter Tomarind brings back invites Nebucheba to visit his parents below, and the crushed datu is never seen again — Tomarind ruling with justice and equity for many years.
summary.zh: 達圖尼布徹巴覬覦勇士托馬林的美妻，兩度設局害之：取怪獸看守的魔法石球；再命他『送信給住地底神域的雙親』——實是誘入井中、以堆石活埋。蒂普卡的女巫授他魔杖，並挖通兩井間的秘密地道。托馬林帶回的『回信』竟邀達圖下井探親——石落人亡，尼布徹巴永不復見；托馬林以公正之道統治多年。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Garcia narrator (Mexico, Pampanga), who says it is an old Pampangan tale; archival record. Fansler knows no variants and judges it 'pretty evidently... old tribal Pampangan tradition'; the witch's rites are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: Before the Spanish occupation there were in the Philippines many petty kingdoms headed by native princes known as datus. Luzon, the scene of countless ravages and hard fightings of warlike tribes, was the home of Datu Nebucheba. His kingdom — at first only a few square miles — was greatly extended by the labor of his young brave warrior, Tomarind. Tomarind had a very beautiful wife, with whom Datu Nebucheba fell in love; but the ruler kept his vile desire secret in his heart for many years, and many times he thought of getting rid of his warrior Tomarind, and thus getting possession of his beautiful wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Tomarind was sent on a dangerous errand: he was ordered to get an enchanted marble ball from one of the caves in a certain mountain, where two monsters of terrible aspect, whose joy was the burning of villages and whose delight was the killing of human beings, guarded the entrance — many persons had entered the door of that death-chamber, but nobody had come from it alive. Suspicious of the coming danger, Tomarind did not go directly to the cave; he sought the famous witch of Tipuca and told her about his situation. Immediately the witch performed a sort of diabolical ceremony, gave Tomarind a magic cane, and sent him away — and when he reached the cave, those that guarded the cave received Tomarind very kindly, and delivered the enchanted marble ball to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'To-morrow, the wife of Tomarind will be mine,' said Nebucheba to himself — 'Alas for him! Very early the next morning Tomarind presented the marble ball to Datu Nebucheba. How quickly he executed my orders! What shall I do to destroy this brave man? The next time he will not escape the danger. I will ask him to take a letter to my parents, who are living under ground, in the realm of the spirits.' The datu caused a well to be dug, and big stones to be piled near the mouth of it; when everything was ready, he summoned the brave warrior, gave him the letter, and told him to start the next morning. Tomarind went again to the witch of Tipuca: 'This is a very great task; but never mind! You will get even with Datu Nebucheba.' That night the witch, with the help of unseen spirits, made a subterranean passage connecting the bottom of the datu's well with that of Tomarind's. 'Nebucheba will ask you to go down into his well; and as soon as you are at the bottom, he will order that the pile of stones be thrown on you. Lose no time, but go in to the subterranean passage that I have prepared for you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, Nebucheba firmly believed that Tomarind was dead, and there was great rejoicing in the datu's house; in the evening, while the revelry was going on, Tomarind appeared with the pretended answer from Nebucheba's parents. The letter read, 'We wish you to come and see us here. We have a very beautiful girl for you.' Nebucheba was greatly surprised, and made up his mind to go down into the well the next day; he gathered all his subjects together and said to them, 'I am going to see my parents. If the place there is better than the place here, I shall not come back. Tomarind will be my successor.' In the morning Nebucheba's subjects took him to the well and lowered him slowly into it; when he reached the bottom, Tomarind threw big stones down on him, and Nebucheba was crushed to death — the people never saw him again. Tomarind became datu, and he ruled his subjects with justice and equity for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.
